THREE-CORNERED TRADE.
Cincinnati, St. Louis and Detroit All
Dickering for Players.
A special from St. Louis, says there
is every indication (hat the Robinsons
will close n deal within the next few
days whereby Catcher Bergen, Pitcher j
Poole arid Fist Baseman Berkley of the i
Cincinnati Reds will be members of the I
1904 Cardinals. The swap, as planned, '
means the transfer of Bergen, Poole j
and Berkley from Cincinnati to the St.
Louis Nationals; the transfer of
Barclay and Burke to the Detroit
(American League) club for cash, and the
sale of "Oy" Seymour, the Reds'
eccentric centerfielder, to the New York
Giants for $5000.

At present the Cincinnati club is
having trouble convincing the St. Louis
club that it would be benelited by the .
deal. Detroit wants Burke and Bar- ;
clay and Cincinnati is willing to give j
St. Louis Berkley, Bergen and perhaps !
Poole.
Kt. Louis would not mind giving up
Barclay, but, strange to state, the
Robinsons do not seem willing to part
iwlth Burke. The Robinsons say they
have not had a satisfactory third
baseman in many years before they
captured Burke from Pittsburg, and that
they must be sure of having another
third baseman in camp before parting
with Burke. There the matter stands.

As soon as the Robinsons are willing
to toss in Burke the papers will be
signed and the three-cornered swap
completed.
Before leaving for Chicago, to attend
the American League meeting.
Magnate Robert L. Hedges of the Browns
gave out the following statement,
showing that a big shakeup is coming
in the St. Louis team:
"I am not knocking any member of
my band," said Hedges, "but, barring j
Powell, Sudholf, Wallace, Burkett and j
Hill, there is not one who is sure of his j
job next summer.

"We want a pennant, or at the worst,
a winning team for World's Fair year.
We know how strong Boston was last ]
season and know that Collins' nine is
not going to be any weaker next
summer. -
"We also appreciate the strength of
Cleveland, New York and the
Athletics. In fact, Detroit and Chicago I

won't be so awful rank, and Johnson Is
busy helping out Washington, so 1 have
got to look out and see that we are not i
lost in the shuffle. I
"Providing that we can get what we >
want in return, we will do a lot of i
trading. We have four catchers and '
one or two of them can be used for
swapping purposes.
"Theft we do not need all the
pitchers that are under contract to us. We
also harbor an extra inflelder and an
extra outfielder. We are surely long on
trading material, and barring Powell,
Suahoff. Wallace, Burkett and Hill, I
do not think we have a player whom
MoAleer would not let figure in a deal.

"Our stars must shine or out they
go."
PRICE TOO SMALL.
The Vatican Orders Not Satisfied with
Money for Friars' Lands.
Rome, Dec. IS. - Considerable
excitement prevailed in the mother houses of
ihe Dominincans, Augustinians,
Franeescans and Recollects over the
announcement of the settlement of the
friars' lands question in the
Philippines.
While the fact that a settlement had
been arrived at was announced to the
heads of the orders by the Vatican, the
orders learned from The Associated
Press correspondent the price,
$7,250,000 to be paid. The frairs were glad
the negotiations had been concluded,
but they think the orders got little for
the lands, as what they originally
asked, $12,000,000, was, they declare,
under the estimated value of the lands,
the value of which had been much
increased, especially since the American
occupation of the Philippines and the
re-establishment of order in the
archipelago.

The friars claim the money they will
receive is scarcely enough to pay
what they borrowed when they were
deprived of everything by the
revolution. Besides, they point out that only
part of the money will go to the friars
as the lauds were really transferred
to private companies, although the
frairs retained a large number of
shares in them.
Tin* Augustinians had their lands
transferred to a company formed in

Madrid, by the Maruis Di Comillias,
the head of the Spanish
Trans-Atlantic Navigation Co. The Dominicans
suceeeeded in so thoroughly concealing
their ownership of land that the
Vatican itself threatened to punish them
severely for having tried to deceive
even the ecclesiastical authorities.
A NEW FLYING MACHINE
Said to Have Had a Successful Trial
Near Kitty Hawk, N. C.
Norfolk, Va., Dec. is. - A successful trial
't a flying machine was made, yesterday,
near Kitty ilawk. X. by Wilbur arid
h ville Wright of Dayton. Ohio. The
machine ilcw for throe miles in the face of «
wind Mowing at the registered velocity
nt .'1 miles an hour, and then gracefully
descended to earth at the spot selected by
the man in the navigator's ear as a
suitable landing place. The machine has no
balloon attachment but gets its force from

propellers worked by a small engine.
Preparatory to its flight the machine
was placed upon a piatforip near Kitt
Hawk. Tills platform was built on a high
sand hill, and when all was in readiness
the fastenings to ihe machine weie
released and it started down an incline.
The navigator. Wilbur Wright, then
started a small gasoline engine which
worked the propellers. When the. end oi
'he incline was reached the machine
gradually arose until it obtained an altitude
of BO feet. In the fact of the strong wind
blowing it maintained an even speed ot
eight miles an hour.

The idea of the box kite had been
adhered to in the basis formation of the
living machine. A huge f ram work of lighl
limbers 33 feet wide, live feet deep and
across top, forms the machine proper.
This is covered with a touch but light
canvass in the center is the navigator's
car and suspended just below the bottom
pi in is a small gasoline engine which
furnishes the motive power for the
propelling and elevating wheels. There
noiwo six-bladed propellers, one arranged
just below the center of the frame so
guaged as to exert an upward force when
in motion, and the other extends
horizontally to the rear from the center of
the ear, furnishing the forward impetus.

Protruding from tlie center of the car
is a huge fan-shaped rudder of canvass
stretcher upon a frame of wood. This
•■udder is controlled by the navigator and
may be moved to each side, raised or
lowered.

? The Alexandretta affair has been
settled by an agreement on the part of
the Turkish government to apologize
to Consul Davis. The state department
at Washington made arrangements
to send Consul Davis back to
Alexandretta in a warship, and the
Turks saw proper to make the most of
an unpleasant situation and say no
more about it. Consul Davis returned
on board the San Francisco.
? All military Paris rings with the
news that Dreyfus has won his nine
years fight for honor and will re-enter
the French army for promotion.

Though there is no official announcement
yet, it is stated on high authority
that the war office has decided that he
shall be re-instated and the details of
his rehabilitation have gone so far that
the regiment he is going to command

with a lieutenant has been secured.
Any officer who expresses disapproval
of the government's act will be dealt
with vigorously. Every element that
goes toward fully establishing the dignity
of the persecuted man has been
thoroughly prepared.

? Charlotte Observer: It seems
strange to read of Rev. Edward Everett
Hale of Boston, being elected chaplain
of the United States senate. He
is the most distinguished Unitarian
preacher in the United States. His

election was procured through the influence
of Senator Hoar of Massachusetts,
who is, we believe, the only Unitarian
in the senate. The Unitarians
are of two classes, both denying the
doctrine of the trinity. The orthodox,
however, believe in the miracles of the
New Testament and the resurrection;
the more progressive and the larger
class reject the resurrection and regard
Christ as a mere man though a perfect
one, accept His code of morals and believe
that He died a martyr. It seems j
strange, we repeat, that a man, however
able and eloquent, of either of
these schools of thought, should be
elected chaplain of the senate.

was made last Thursday near
Kitty Hawk, N. C., by Wilbur and
Orville Wright of Dayton, O., says a
letter from Norfolk, Va. The machine
flew for three miles in the face of a
wind blowing at the registered velocity
of twenty-one miles an hour, and then
gracefully descended to earth at the
spot selected by the men in the navigator's
car as a suitable landing place.

Tha marhlro has n r\ hallr?r>n
attach
ment, but gets Its force from propellers
worked by a small engine. Preparatory
to its flight the machine was
placed upon a platform near Kitty
Hawk. This platform was built on a
high sand hill, and when all was in
readiness the fastenings to the machine
were released and it started down an
incline. The navigator, Wilbur Wright,
then started a small gasoline engine
which worked the propellers. When
the end of the incline was reached the
machine gradually rose until it obtained
an altitude of sixty feet. In the
face of the strong wind blowing. It
maintained an even speed of eight
miles an hour. The idea of the box
kite has been adhered to in the basic
formation of the flying machine. A
huge frame work of light timbers, thirty-three
feet wide, Ave feet deep and
five feet across the top, forms the machine

proper. This is covered with a
tough, but light, canvas. In the centre,
and suspended just below the
bot

torn plan. Is the small gasoline engine,
which furnishes the motive power for
the propelling and elevating wheels.
There are two slx-bladed propellers,
one arranged just below the centre of
the frame, so gauged as to exert an
upward force when In motion, and the
other extends horizontally to the rear
from the centre of the car, furnishing
the forward Impetus. Protruding from
the centre of the car Is a huge fanshaped
rudder of canvas, stretched upon
a frame of wood. This rudder Is
controlled by the navigator and may
be mov .J to each side, raised or lowered.

No test was made today of the
flying machine. The Wright brothers
will leave tomorrow for uayion 10
spend the holidays, and will return to
Kitty Hawk after New Tear's to perfect
their invention.

Although there is a strong probability
of war between the United States
and Colombia it will not amount to a
great deal either as to the shedding of
blood or destruction of property. One
thoroughly efficient regiment of the
United States army would probably
be more than a match for the whole
Colombian nation, and it is quite probable
that the Colombians thoroughly
understand the fact, but nevertheless
they will have to fight a little. The
brutal manner in which the tremendous
power of the United States has been
used is as insufferable to them as it
is cowardly in us. By spilling a little
of their blood they can get a certain
amount of vindication; but for us
Americans, there is nothing but repudiation
of the unwarranted action of
the president, or lasting shame.

Senator Morgan is beginning to make
it appear that the real object of the
president's monkey business down in
Panama was to defeat the construction
of the canal rather than to further
the work. There is no doubt of the
right of the Colombians to drive such
a trade as they saw proper, and inability
to secure what we want by purchase
and persuasion does not give us
the right to resort to force. We cannot
justify ourselves even with the argument
that Colombia should not be
allowed to stand in the way of the
worl Vs progress. This argument
wouk be fairly justifiable if the Panama
ro -te were the only route or even
undisputably the most practicable.

But the fact remains that the Nicaragua
route is not only as good or better;
but it Is available whenever we shall
choose to take possession of it. We
hope to see the canal constructed; but
unless the work can be accomplished
without dishonor on the part of the
United States, it will do more harm
than good.

Russia and Japan.
While it is certain that relations between
Russia and Japan are exceedingly
strained, and that a grave crisis
is at hand, the question as to whether
it will be peace or war remains for future
developments.
Control of Korea and the Liao Tung
peninsular is the issue at stake. Russia
considers that her future existence
depends upon the success of her plans
in this direction, and Japan feels that
Russia's success means hfer ruin.

The controversy has been on for several
years, in fact ever since the close
of the Chino-Japanese war of 1894. It
will be remembered that Japan defeated
China and compelled her to cede all
claims to the Liao Tung peninsular.
Russia, however, stepped In at about
that time and, backed by Germany and
France, vetoed the arrangement.
Japan was terribly humiliated; but
being unable to cope with such an alliance
as that with which she was
confronted, was obliged to submit. But
even then it was with much reservation
and a feeling that some day she
would be able to demand and enforce
her rights. Since then both Russia and
Japan have been exerting themselves

to get the best or eacn other in ine
extension of national influence In Korea, t
and this has been the basis of existing '
trouble. r
The principal reason why war has a
not broken out long ago Is a lack of a
money. The finances of Japan have v
been in a bad way almost ever since v
the inception of her modernized gov- r
ernment, and she is unable to buy the s
war materials necessary to cope with 1
Russia. Russia is in the same position. ?

Because of the extent of her interests t
and ambitions she would not have hes- t
itated an instant to attempt the punishment
of her annoying "big little" antagonist
had it not been for the fact r
that her ministers know that her fl- u
nancial ruin might easily result. ^
But notwithstanding the situation f
outlined, it is hardly safe to say that i:
the danger of war between these two j
countries is slight. As great as are t
the handicaps of both there need be no e
occasion for surprise if they should be c
at each other's throats within the next !,
few months or even within the next v
few days. a

RED CHIEF'S PASSING.
Famous indian Leader Said to be
Nearing the End at Pine Ridge.
Red Cloud. the famous Indian chief.
who was second in command of the
aborigines to Sitting Bull at the
battle of the Little Big Horn, when
Geperal Custer and all his men were
massacred. is lying at the point of
death at Pine Ridge, 8. D., says a cor.
respondent of the Chicago Tribune.
His condition is regarded as hopeless
and probably ere many days he will
have gone to the happy hunting
grounds of his fathers.

For many years past Red Cloud has
been mentioned among (the "good
Indians".of the nation. Since the peace
that followed the final defeat of his
tribe he has been the white man's
friend and has received many
attentions from the officials at
Washington, which city he twice visited in the
interests of those over whom he once
ruled with an iron hand.
Next to Tecumseh. he has filled the
largest place in American history of
any Indian, and in many respects he
was that gallant warrior's superior.

His compatriot, Sitting Bull, was
more notoiious. but his stauding
among the Sioux themselves was far
below that of the truly great man who
now lies at the verge of the grave.

Viewed in the light of subsequent
developments. Red Cloud's position
was entirely correct. The white men
who flocked to the frontier made no
distinction between Indians who were
hostile and those who were friendly.
Moreover, a total Ignorance of Indian
manners and customs and of travel
on the plains brought about many
conflicts and misunderstandings between
the Indians and well meaning and
respectable settlers on route to Califor.
nia. Scores of Instances of this
character could easily be gathered, and
certainly should be published as a
part of the history of the plains. It
is not surprising then, to find that
from 1848 to 1877 continual war was
waged upon the plains. These thirty
years of conflict, looked at from a
military standpoint, comprised a long
series of petty skirmishes and
massacres perpetrated by both white and
red men alike. Viewed from the
Indian standpoint, it was a continual

struggle on the part of some 4,000 or
5,000 men against InVasion and
extermlnation. The result, as we all know,
was the almost total annlhliation of
the Indian.

DEBATE ON CANAL QUESTION.
Senators Think Recognition of Panama
Republic Was Somewhat Impetuous.
Washington , Dec. 17. - The senate
today was the scene of important
debate on the isthmian canal question
as affected by the president's
recognition of the republic of Panama.
Discussion began with a speech by Mr.
Hoar on his resolution of inquiry and
lasted several hours.
In addition to Mr. Hoar's address
there were speeches by Mr. Gorman
and Mr. Foraker. All three were
notable utterances and of historical
interest. Mr. Hoar confined his
remarks to his resolution, and they were
carefully written out and read from
manuscript. He held that this
country has not yet received full offici;il
information concerning the isthmian
revolution, and criticised in sharp
terms the conduct of this country as
shown by what has been given out.

He characterized the conduct of the
United States as that of a policeman
who would manacle a man who was
about to be attacked for robbery and
who would then insist on having the
spoils of the theft delivered to
himself.
There were no reservations in Mr.
Gorman's utterances. He especially
alleged that the situation in Colombia
had been created to make a campaign
issue, and charged Assistant
Secretary of State Loomis with violation of
the proprieties in discussing the situ
ation at a banquet in New York. He
also insisted that unless further light
was thrown on the situation he would
oppose the Panama treaty. He also
referred to the impetuous action of the
executive, and declared that the senate
should oppose the jeopardizing of the
interests of the country.

Mr. Foraker took Mr. Hoar to task
severely for hia remarks reflecting: on
the administration, and his
indiscretion in speaking in open session
concerning executive matters. He
defended the administration for ita atti
tude toward the Panama revolt.

Land Commissioners Meet.
Washington , Dec. 17. - The
commission on public lands recently
appointed by President Roosevelt to
report on the condition, operation and
effect of the present land laws and on
the use, condition, disposal and
settlement of the public lands, held its
first meeting today. Arrangements
were made to carry forward promptly
and effectively the work for which the
commission was appointed, aud with
that end in view, beginning next
Tuesday, meetings will be held daily
except Saturday at the general land
office for the purpose of considering the
various matters which will come
before the commissioners. Mr. Richards
will be chairman of the committee.

Sugar Duty is Affected.
Washington , Dec. 17. - The
president signed the Cuba reciprocity bill
a few minutes before 1 o'clock this
afternoon. Now that the bill has
become a law, a question of great
interest has arisen, namely, the effect of
the reduction of the duty on Cuban
sugar under the importations of sugar
from other countries.
The British government has served
formal notice upon the state
department that under the favored-nation
clause it expects that British sugar
from the West Indies shall be
admitted into the United States on equal
terms with Cuban sugar and it is not
doubted that Germany, France,
xVustria and the other great beet sugar
producing countries will do likewise.

An old holding of Attorney General
Olney under President Cleveland's
administration was adverse to such
demands. but the question promises to
be reopened with vigor.
Armed Men Protect Treasure.
New Yokk , Dec. 17. - Armed
detectives formed part of the crew of an
express train from New York for
Boston, which left here about midnight.
The train had a cargo valued at a
round million, including a large sum
in gold.
Tne armed escort traveling in a
special train was sent out because of
threats said to have been received by
officials of the Adams Express
company that unless a certain large
amount of money was forthcoming the
train would be robbed.

An Idaho Murder Mystery.
Hope , Idaho, Dec. 17. - The body of
Michael Sweeney, foreman for Twohy
& Guthrie at railroad camp No. 1,
was brought here last night pending
investigation by the coroner into his
death. Sweeney was shot down in
cold blood yesterday afternoon by an
unknown assassin. He had just
completed his dinner and was about to

call the men to work when a shot was
fired, apparently from a nearby brush.
Sweeney fell mortally wounded, dying
in a few minutes. So far as known
Sweeney had no enemies and the
tragedy is clothed in mystery.
To Open Crow Reservation.
Washington , Dec.
17. - -Congressman Dixon has introduced a bill for
the opening of the Crow reservation.
The bill as introduced follows the
general lines as the bills heretofore
prepared, but placing the valuation at $3
an acre on farming land to be thrown
open to homestead settlers only.
Timber and stone entries are not to be
permitted. Homestead entrymen must
pay 50 cents an acre when the filing is
made, and 50 cents an acre a year
until full payment has been made.

At the end of four years all lands
remaining unsold will be offered for
sale to the highest bidder in tracts of
320 acres each at a minimum price of
$1.25 an acre. This new bill has been
framed to meet the objections
heretofore urged by Speaker Cannon.
ADVANCE IN RAILROAD RATES.
Report of Interstate Commerce
Commission Gives Interesting Information.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 18. - The
seventeenth annual report of the interstate
commerce commission was transmitted
to congress today. The preliminary
income account for the year ending
June 30, 1903, shows railroad returns
for 201,457 miles of line, which is
approximately 98 per cent of the entire
mileage in the United States.

The report says one of the most
significant things in railway operations
for the past three years has been the
marked and general advance in rates.
Such increase applies in almost all
sections of the country and to all
kinds of traffic. These increases are
general and they amount in the
aggregate to an enormous sum. The effect
of these advances has been to
correspondingly increase the tax laid upon
the general body of producers and
consumers in this country for the
benefit of the owners of railway property.

These advances have been usually, if
not always, the result of concerted
action by the carriers.
Without expressing an opinion as
to whether the action of these carriers
has amounted to a violation of the
law, the commission desires to point
out the fact that such action does
prevail as practically eliminates all
competition in the tariff rates. The
requirement of the law that carriers
shall compete affords no protection to
the public.
While railway managers insist that
these advances have been justified by
increased cost of operation, the
commission says that the great increase
in the amount of traffic, together with
many economics in operation has
enabled railroads, as a matter of fact,
to handle it cheaper in proportion.

The commission sees no assurance of
a decline in rates in the future.
The commission refers again to the
evils resulting from excessive
payments by railroad companies for the
use of private cars, and recommend
that the payment of car mileage for
their use be regulated. The report
calls attention to the importance of a
trustworthy valuation of railway
property, and recommends that the
congress take this mtater under
advisement.

Nebraska Senator Indicted.
Omaha , Dec. 17. - The United States
grand jury made its report to the
court, returning 19 true bills. These
included indictments against United
States Senator Chas. H. Deitrich for
the illegal leasing of a building to the
government to be used as a postoffice.
Senator Dietrich is charged with the
alleged violation of section 3739 of
the revised statutes, which provides
that no member or delegate to
congress shall "directly or indirectly,
undertake, execute, hold or enjoy, in
whole or in part, any contract or
agreement made or entered into in
behalf of the United States, by any
officer or person authorized to make
contracts on behalf of the United States."
The indictment charges that Senator
Deitrich leased to the government on
April 24, 1901, a building at Hastings,
Neb., to b3 used for a postoffice, at

an annual rental of $1,300.
Mother Starved for Children
ST. Paul , Dec. 18. - Mrs. Geneva
Flaherty died on a Northern Pacific
train coining' into this city today irom
Duluth from starvation and exposure.
She had four children, aged from 15

TO OPEN FLATHEAD RESERVE.
Congressman Dixon Introduces a Bill to
Make Lands Subject to Settlement.
Washington , Dec.
16. - Congressman Dixon introduced a bill today in
the house for the opening of the
Flathead Indian reservation. The bill is
along a new line for opening In .,
dian reservations. Heretofore the
method of procedure has always been
first, a treaty with the Indians, but
under a decision of the supreme court,
of last January, in the Lone Wolf
case, the court held power is vested in
congress to administer Indian
reservations as congress saw fit.

Dixon's bill provides for immediate
survey and allotment of the land, the
appointment of a commission,
consisting of two members of the tribe, two
citizens of Montana and one special
agent of the department, to appraise
and classify the lands. Appraisment
will run from $1.25 to $5 per acre.
Settlement can be made only by
qualified homesteaders in payments for
their lands in five annual payments.
Timber land will be appraised and
sold to the highest bidder for cash,
After five years, all lands not taken
will be sold to the highest bidder f or
cash, in lots not exceeding 320 acres.

The law takes effect only in the event
of its ratification by the majority of
adult males now holding tribal rela'
tions The area affected by the bill
is 2,500,000 acres.

A Successful Airship Test.
Norfolk , Va., Dec. 18. - A success
ful trial of a flying machine has been
made near Kitty Hawk, N. C., by
Wilbur and Orville Wright, of Day-!
ton, O. The machine flew for three
miles in the face of a wind blowing at
the registered velocity of ten miles an
hour and then gracefully descended to
earth at the spot selected by the
navigator. The machine has no balloon
attachment, but gets its force from
propellers worked by a small engine.

The idea of the box kite has been
adhered to in the basic formation of
the flying machine. A huge
framework of light timbers thirty-five feet
wide, five feet deep and five feet across
the top forms the machine proper.
This is covered with a tough but light
canvas. In the center is the
navigator's car, and suspended just below
the bottom plan is a small gasoline
engine, which furnished the motive
power for the propelling and elevating;

acrosscut a quantity of debris and waste

defendants the alternative of submitting

county jail of Lewis and Clarke

complied with.

3, issued by J udge Knowles, satisfies

marshal be present at the time and

complied with, the marshal shall begin
the enforcement of the judgment
pronounced by Judge Beatty.

conditions of the money market during
the past few months, just at a time
when the movement of livestock was
heaviest, millions of dollars have been
lost to the stockerovvers' followers.

many instances called in their loans
besides declining to make new ones,
thereby depriving stockmen of ueces-1
sary funds with which to protect their
interests.

Colombia Receives Advice.
Washington , Dec. 21. - Diplomatic
pressure will be brought to bear upon
Colombia by several European
powers to prevent war between that
country and the United States. The first
step in this direction already has been
taken by several foreign powers
through their representatives here
who have informed General Rafael
Reyes of the futility of any attempt by
Colombia to retake Panama,
declaring that it will result only in
precipitating the Bogota government into
war with the United States aud said to
him that the result of such acts was a
catastrophe Colombia herself must
realize.

Nine Killed In Wreck
Kansas City , Mo., Dec. 21. - The
Meteor, the fast train on the St. Louig
»Sc San Francisco, was wrecked at
Godfrey, fifteen miles south of Fort
Scott, Kan., early this morning. The
train ran into a switch, and all cara
except the sleeper were derailed and
turned over. Eight persons were
killed and 32 injured. The crew of a
freight train that had preceded the
Meteor left the switch open and the
passenger train jumped the track and
rolled down a slight embankment. All
save the sleeper turned over" and so
fast was the train running that the
engine and forward baggage car landed
nearly sixty feet off the roadbed
before they stopped.

A MACHINE THAT FLIES.
The Wright Brothers Declare that
They Have Solved the Problem
of Navigating the Air.
"Dayton, O., Jar. 6.-The Wright
-brothers, inventors ot' the flying'
machine which has attracted such
widespread attention, have prepared
the following, which they say is the
first correct statement cf the successful
trials made by them:
"On the morning of Dec. 17, between
10.30 and noon, four flights were made,
two by Orville Wright and two by Wil?
bur Wright. The starts were ail made
from a point on the level and about
200 feet west of our camp, which is
situated a quarter of a mile north of
Kill Devil Sand, in Dare county, N.

C. The wind at the time of the flight
had a velocity of 27 miles an hour at
10 o'clock and 24 miles an hour at
noon as recorded by the anemometer
at the Kitty Hawk weather bureau
station. This anemometer is 30 feet
from the ground. Our own measure?
ments, made with an anemometer at a
height of fbur feet from the ground,
showed a velocity of about 22 miles
when the first flight was made and
22f^ when the last flight was made.

The flight was made directly against
the wind. Each time the machine
started from the level ground by its
own power with no ssistance from
gravity or other source whatever.
After a run of about 40 feet along the
monorail track which held the ma?
chine eight inches from the groundd,
it rose from the track and under th&
direction of the operator climbed up?
ward on an inclined course until a
height of eight or ten feet from the
ground was reached, after which the
course was kept as near horizontal as
the wind gusts and the limited skill
of the operator would permit. Into
the teeth of a 25-mile gale the 'flyer'
made its way forward with a speed of
10 miles an hour over the ground and
30 to 35 miles an hour through the air.

It had previusiy been decided that for
reasons of personal safety these first
trials should be made as close to the
ground as possible. The height chosen
was scarcely sufficient for
manoeuvering in so gusty a wind and with no
previous acquaintance with the con?
duct of the machine and its controll?
ing mechanism. Consequently the first
flight was short. The succeeding
flights rapidly increased in length and
at the fourth trial a flight of 59 sec?
onds was made in which the machine
flew a little more than half a mile
through the air and a distance of more
than 852 feet over the ground. The
landing was due to a slight error o?

judgment on the part of the operator.
After passing over a little hummock
of sand in attempting to bring the
machine down to the desired height
the operator turned the rudder too far
and the machine turned downward
more quickly than had been expected.
The reverse movement of the rudder
was a fraction of a second too late to
prevent the machine from touching
the ground and thus ending the flight.
The whole occurrence occupied little
if any more than one second of time.

"Only those who are acquainted
with practical aeronautics can appre?
ciate the difficulties in attempting the
first trials of a flying machine in a
25mile gale. As winter had already set
in, we would have postponed our
trials to a more favorable season, but
for the fact that we were determined
before returning home to as?
certain whether the machine
possessed sufficient power to
withstand the shock of landing and of
sufficient capacity of control to make
a flight safe in boisterous winds as
well as in calm air. When the points
had been defiaately established we at
once packed our goods and returned
home, knowing that the age of the fly?

ing machine had come at last.
"From the beginning we have em?
ployed entirely new principles of con?
trol and as all the experiments have
been conducted at our own expense
without assistance from any individ?
ual or institution, we do now feel
ready at present to give cut any pic?
ture or detailed description of the ma?
chine. "

Cause and Transmission of Texas
Cattle Fever.
Nothing positive was known in re?

gard to either the cause of the disease
of the manner of its transmission until
the subject was taken up by the Bureau
of Animal Industry in 1889. Under
the general supervision of Dr. D. E.
Salmon, chief of the bureau, a sys?
tematic investigation of the subject
was begun at the experiment station,
near the city of Washington. In the
laboratories of the station, one cf the
best pieces of biological research that
this country has witnessed was carried
on by Dr. Theobald Smith, chief of
the Division of Animal Pathology,
now a member of the Harvard medi
cal faculty. One of the most charac?

teristic symptoms of Texas fever in its
acute stages is the loss of blood,
which, passing off with the urine, has
given to the disease, in some coun?
tries, the name of "red-water." It
has also been observed that the kid?
neys, liver, and especially the spleen
were greatly enlarged and engorged
with blood, from which fact the dis?
ease is sometimes known as "splenetic
fever." But Dr. Smith now demon?
strated that the fever is not primarily
a disease of these organs, but of the
blood. He discovered the presence of
a -micro-parasite in the red corpuscles
of the blood, by which the corpuscle
itself is destroyed. There is an
enormus multiplication of these parasites
during the earlier stages of the dis?

ease, resulting in the destruction of
one-fourth to three-fourths of the red
corpuscles. These dead corpuscles are
eliminated through the kidneys, and
give rise to the characteristic symp?
toms of the disease. The same micro?
organism was found in the blood of
healthy Southern cattle.
While these discoveries were being
made in the laboratories, equally im?
portant results were reached in the
field experiments that were "being car?
ried on at the same time. Under the
immediate direction of Dr. F. L.
Kilbourne, a series of experiments was
carried on, covering a period of three
years, for the purpose of determining
what part, if any, the cattle tick has
in the transmission of Texas fever.

From these experiments several im?
portant facts were definately establish?
ed. It appeared that the plague always
broke cut among Northern cattle
when they were allowed to run on pas- 1
tn res occupied by "ticky" Southern1
cattle, or over which ticks picked
from Southern cattle had-been scatter- j
ed. The same results were obtained
when ticks were transferred directly
from Southern to Northern cattle. Not
only so, but even young ticks hatched
artificially, which had never been in !
contact with Southern cattle, were j
found to transmit the fever when they j
were applied to Northern cattle or I
were scattered over the pasture occu- j
pied by them. On the other hand,
Southern cattle '.vere found to be
entirely harmless if carefully cleared of
ticks before being placed in the same
pastures with the Northern animals.

It was proved that the fever could net
be contracted by taking rho germs in?
to the digestive tract, for large quan?
tities Gf ticks wore fed to susceptible
animals along with their food with?
out the lep.st sign of the disease. On
the other hand, it was found that the
disease could be readily transmitted
by inoculating susceptible animals
j with the blood drawn directly from
! the veins of cows suffering from the
disease, cr with the blood drawn from
the veins of healthy Southern cattle,
thus proving that the disease germs are
always present in the blood ol' immune
Soutiiern cattle, lt is of interest to
note, in connection with the tick
theory, that the transmission of dis?

ease germs by means of parasites,
then entirely new, is now familiar to
us all through t!.e discovery thar tho j
mosquito is responsible for the spread I
of malaria and yellow fever.-From
"rho Texas Cattle Fever: How Scien?
ce is Winning a Long Fight,"' by Pro?
fessor Charles Shirley Potts, in the
Am,-rican Monthly Review of Reviews
for January.

TO LAUNCH TODAY.
Four Masted Schooner Henry F. Kreger
To Be Sent Overboard.
(Special to the PRESS.)
Bath. December IS - The last
launching of the year 1903 takes place
tomorrow noon from the old Reed ship
yard at the south end when Alderman
JJlwell S. Crosby will send overboard
the four masted schooner Henry F.
Kreger, which will be the second one
he has built and launched during the
year.
The Kreger is a double decked vessel
measuring 202 feet in length, 40.2 feet
beam, 21.8 feet depth of hold and has a
tonnage of 1250.

The Kreger is named for the
ninevear-old son of Captain William
kreger of Fairfield, commander of the
six masted schooner Addle M.
Lawrence. Master Kreger will be on hand
tomorrow to christen the vessel with
a large floral bouquet. Upwards of
400 invitations have been issued by
Mr. Crosby and Captain John C.
Darrah, the commander, and it is
expected a large party will lunch
Aboard, including several Portland
Aboard. A lunch will be served In the
' cabin.
Captain Darrah, the commander, is
a native of Richmond, and has
followed the sea all his life. fihving
crossed and re-crosscd tv' -"in
probably 20 times.

ON WATER FRONT.
Belated Steamers Hungarian and
Hurona Arrived.
HAD ROUGH PASSAGES.
Work of Dredging Out at Portland
Pier Begins.
The event of interest along the
water front yesterday was the arrival of
the belated steamer Hibernian of the
Allan line which had been 18 days on
the way from Glasgow to this port,
and the steamer Hurona of the
Thomson line which came in a little In
advance of the Hungarian after a voyage
of 13 days from London. The
Hungarian is making her first voyage to
this port and judging from the fact
that the steamer was several days
longer than the average for a trip
across1 the Atlantic, and from the
testimony of the officers and the looks of
the ship, the steamer had what might
truthfully be called a rough trip. The
Hibernian is commanded by Captain
John M. Wallace and sailed from
Glasgow November 30th. The first
six days the steamer had nothing but
gales to encounter. Several times

heavy seas w'ashed completely over her
and did considerable damage.
Portions of the cattle pens were washed
away several times but no injury was
sustained by the ship Itself. The
Hungarian was badly iced and had
considerable snow on her sides. She brought
over a cargo of 1,600 tons and of this
there was 600 tons of coal for the
Grand Trunk Railway company. She
also had 40 bales of burlap for C. M.
Bailey and two cases of brass wire
cloth for H. & A. Allan. Seven
returning cattlemen were on board. The
Hungarian is a commodious vessel and
is 400 feet In length; 50 feet beam and
30 feet deep and has a net tonnage of
2,770 tons. The steamer Hurona from
London, the other vessel arriving
yesterday, did not have quite as rough a
time as did the Hibernian although

Captain Dorwood says that it was
regular winter weather all the way
over. The steamer sailed, from London
December 5th with a cargo of 4,200
tons of coal which is bekig discharged
at the coal pockets of the Grand Trunk
Railway company. She also brought
110 tons of general freight, all of which
is to go through to Canada. Two
stowaways were on board, two of them
Englishmen and two Norwegians. As
the stowaways could not prove
American citizenship they were sent to the
jail and will be returned to Europe
when the Hurona sails December 26th
unless it may be decided to send them
Saturday on the Cervona of the same
line.

The Italian bark Leone which had
such a hard time getting to Bangor
from Port Labot, Wales, is having a
harder time to get away from Bangor,
a® the ice is fast covering the river.
The bark finished taking on her cargo
of shook on Thursday and the tug
Ralph Ross tried to drag her down to
open water. The steering gear of the
tug became disabled and she was ns
helpless as the ice bound bark. The
tugs Bismarck and Seguin were
ordered from Bath to help out in the
predicament. As soon as the bark Is out,
the river will be closed to navigation as
It will be covered over by Ice in
another day or so.

From news received in this city
yesterday from St. John, N. B., there is a
possibility that the steamer St. Croix
of the Eastern Steamship company,
International division, may be sold. It
is understood that parties desire to buy
her to operate a line on the Pacific
coast. If the deal goes through the
St. Croix will be the second large
Portland steamer that will have to round
the Horn to enter the. Pacific. The
first one to do this was the Cottage
City a few years ago. The St. Croix
is one of the best steamers coming to
this port and is now on the docks in
Boston undergoing repairs. In the
event of the sale of the St. Croix the

steamer Calvin Austin win wnnoui
doubt continue on the Portland, Boston
and St. John route all winter.

? Addressing an audience of 3,000

Broughton, a leading Baptist minister
of Atlanta, Ga., denounced Senator
Tillman's anti-negro views. In the
course of his speech, Dr. Broughton
said: "I heard Senator Tillman on
Friday give his lecture on the negro.
I tried to be fair in .my estimate of it.
For reckless frankness it was a model,
for sensible argument it was a mess.
His whole talk, from start to finish,

people. Never once in his treatment

of the realm of the rankest paganism.

Notwithstanding his politics since
the war there are many Confederate
soldiers who hold that Gen. Longstreet
was one of the ablest generals in the
Confederate service. Some rank him
above Lee and Jackson even. This is
rather too high in our opinion. As we
see it the places of Lee and Jackson
are almost indisputably fixed; but that
Longstreet was an able general, second
to none after the two just mentioned,
there is no reason for general
controversy.

AccoRPfNG to . a Columbia dispatch,
Capt. D. J. Griffith cleared $29,600 on
the two state farms last year. That is
certainly a good showing; but we would
be better satisfied with more complete
details. There has been a tendency in
the past to count receipts as profits,
and say nothing of expenses. For instance
the state furnishes the farms
with everything, labor, stock and provisions,
and sometimes at very heavy
cost. We would like to feel assured
that the $29,600 referred to Is the
amount left over after all bills of all
kinds have been paid. On such a
showing Capt. Griffith will certainly be
entitled to the highest commendation.

As we understand the law; the only
question that Is properly involved in
the case of Antioch church vs. the Jenkins
distillery is whether or not the
distillery is located within two miles
of the church. If the two institutions
are within two miles of each other,
then one of them should be moved.
According to our view, of course, there
is no question as to which. We are
certain that the church has been there
innc.act- hut in the oninlon of the

board this may be a point against it.
There seems to be a pretty strong sentiment
in this state to the effect that
churches have had their day and dispensaries
and distilleries should now
have a show. However, aS matters
now stand, the law is fortunately in
favor of the church, and we presume
that the board will be forced to so decide.
Russia and Japan.
Although conflicting opinions are
still emanating from apparently authentic
sources, the developments of
the past few days seem to have made
more for war than for peace.

The reply of Russia to Japan's last
communication was delivered at Tokio
on Wednesday, and although its terms
have not been made public, the understanding
is that it is not satisfactory
to the Japanese, and that there is now
left nothing for them but action.
Dispatches from Korea bring the
news that on account of the disturbed
condition of affairs in the kingdom,
various foreign governments have
landed marines at different places and
ordered them to the capital. Russia
landed a force of marines a few days
ago and when Japan refused to allow
them to be transported over the railroad
under her control, they were
marched through the country to Seoul.

The movements of the Russian and
Japanese fleets, as reported in the papers
add seriousness to the situation,
and the probability is that within the
next few days there will be news of a
conflict. This seems to be the leading
opinion of all the European capitals.

"I read what was said in The Enquirer
of Tuesday about lap robe
thieves," said a local physician to the
reporter on Thursday, "and," he continued.
"I want to say that I would
like to see some practical plan adopted
to break up the annoying business.

I suggest this. Suppose those of us
who are interested raise a fund, say
something like one hundred dollars for
the prosecution of the thieves. I'll
give ten dollars to such a fund or rather
stand pledge to pay that amount
if necessary, and if other physicians
and liverymen will come into a pool,
I think we can raise an amount that
will be interesting. I have an idea
that If we had a pool of a hundred or
so dollars with the understanding that

we would pay a reward of $20 for the
conviction of each lap robe thief together
with incidental expenses, etc.,
it would not be a great while before
we would be able to leave our lap
robes in our buggies without so much
danger of having them stolen."

false." He said that the only thing
that Jenkins could call an offer to sell
was his statement to him that if he
could not force his nuisance of a distillery
out of the community he would
be compelled to sell his land; that the
rowdiness created by the distillery had
compelled him to send his children into
North Carolina, where he had to pay
tuition whprpaa he nreferred and was

entitled to have them attend the Antloch
school, where he would not have
to pay, but whither he dared not. send
the little ones on account of the
drunkenness along the road.
At the December hearing the prosecution
appeared with an affidavit from
two of the three members of the county
board of dispensary control. At the
hearing yesterday the defense submitted
an affidavit from the member who
had not appeared in the case then, and
a statement * from one of the others
saying that since he had found out the
standing of the third member, who
lived in the section affected, he had
changed his position and now wanted
to be understood as favoring the retention
of the permit.

Mr. Butler admitted that it is probable
that the place lacks about a quarter
of being two miles from the church,
but argued it had been placed in good
faith with the belief that it was far
enough, and pointed out that there was
abundant evidence to be found of this
good faith in the fact that many of
those now petitioning for its removal
had signed his petition for a permit
five years ago.
Mr. J. C. Otts in concluding his argument
said that the board would have
some bad results to answer for if it
continued the permit. He said that
that section would be dotted all over
with small illicit distilleries by men
who are already arguing that if the
state permits a big nuisance like the
Jenkins distillery they are entitled to
run at least small ones, and there was

so much Justice in their position that
he would advise them to go ahead.
Jenkins Wins.
The state board of dispensary directors
has dodged the issue in the case
of Antioch church vs. the Jenkins distillery,
by suggesting that the distillery
go a little further down the
branch. The board's conclusions are
reported in. the Columbia State of this
morning as follows:
The Antioch Baptist church has lost
out in its vigorous three months' fight
before the state board of dispensary
directors against the Jenkins distillery.

But the bone of contention is to be
removed a quarter of a mile further
from the church, in order to put it outside
of the two mile limit. Much feeling
and bitterness have been engendered
by the contest and it is likely
that the church will renew Its fight
against the distiller in the Cherokee
court by bringing specific charges of

\ lumuuu ui mw ubciiiisl 111111.
The following resolutions adopted by
the board yesterday, explain the position
the board has taken in the premises:
Resolved, first, That it is the judgment
of this board that the petitioners
vs. the Jenkins distillery in Cherokee
county have failed to prove that
the Jenkins distillery Is a nuisance to
the community, in that they have failed
to allege and prove any specific violations
of the dispensary law, consequently
we cannot revoke the permit
upon the ground of nuisance.

Second. That after investigating the
books of the revenue oifice we find that
Jenkins has no retail liquor dealer's
license, but that the entry to that effect
as testified to by Mr. McCulley
was a clerical error, hence that charge
does not constitute a prima facie case
against him.
It wati made to appear and is not denied
that the distillery is within two
miles ol* a church in contravention of
the law. and it is ordered: That unless
the said Jenkins removes his distillery
beyond the two mile limit from
a church or school house as is provided
by law, and within the confines of
Cherokee township in the county of
Cherokee, by the first day of February,
1904, his permit to distill alcoholic
liquors shall stand revoked.

Death of Mrs. W. E. Jackson.
Mrs. W. E. Jackson died at her
home about four miles northwest of
Yorkville last Wednesday morning at
7.30 o'clock, after an illness of only a
few days. The funeral took place at
Union Baptist church, of which she
was a member, on Thursday, the services
being conducted by Rev. W. E.
Hurt. She leaves a husband and three
children.
Death of Dr. R. A. Crawford.
Dr. Robert A. Crawford died at his
home near Smith's Turnout, in Chester
county, last Sunday morning, of
heart failure. He arose and dressed
himself as usual, and death came suddenly
a few minutes afterward. Dr.

Crawford was a son of the late James
E. Crawford and a brother of Captain
E. A. Crawford and Mrs. Aggies I.
Moore of Yorkvllle, also of Mrs. J. M.
McFadden of Chester. He was born In '
the neighborhood of the spot where he !
spent his life, about seventy-eight
years ago, and was twice married, the
first time, to Miss Amanda Wherry and
the second time to Miss Marlon Williams,
both of the same neighborhood.
He studied medicine previous to the
war, and was a graduate of the South '<
Carolina medical college; but he prac- |
tlced only a short time. Immediately j
after the breaking out of the war, he 1

went to the front as a sergeant In the
Calhoun Guards of Chester, and served
until the second battle of Manassas, In
which he participated as Captain of
Company F, Sixth South Carolina volunteers.
As the result of severe
wounds received In this battle, he secured
a discharge from the service.
Dr. Crawford was widely known In
both York and Chester counties and
stood high In the estimation of his
many acquaintances as a man of sterling
worth and high Integrity. He
was kind-hearted and true In all his
relations with his fellow citizens. For
irany years previous to his death he
was a member of Bethesda Presbyterian
church, and his body was Interred
In the cemetery there on Tuesday.
